title: Title Clearance and Lien Resolution Requirements — CTL Policy
content:
Title and Lien Resolution Policy — Clear-To-List Requirements for Title Clearance.

Purpose: Clear and marketable title is a fundamental prerequisite for listing any property. A title defect discovered after listing can result in failed closings, legal disputes, and reputational damage. This policy establishes the title verification and lien resolution standards for CTL determination.

Section 1 — Title Search Requirements:
A title search must be performed or refreshed within 60 days of the CTL determination date. The title search must cover a minimum of the most recent 24-month period and must identify: (a) current ownership chain confirming the seller (servicer or asset owner) holds title, (b) all recorded liens and encumbrances against the property, (c) any active lis pendens filings, (d) any judgments recorded against the current or former owner that may attach to the property, (e) any pending probate or estate proceedings affecting title, and (f) easements and restrictions of record.

Section 2 — Lien Classification and CTL Impact:

First Mortgage Lien: Should have been extinguished by the foreclosure sale. Verify the trustee's deed or sheriff's deed was properly recorded and the prior mortgage is reflected as foreclosed in the title records. If the first mortgage lien still appears as open, a lien release or satisfaction must be recorded.

Junior Liens (second mortgages, HELOCs): In non-judicial foreclosure states, junior liens are typically extinguished by foreclosure of the senior lien. However, the personal obligation may survive. Verify with the title company that all junior liens have been addressed. Any junior lien that survived foreclosure (for example, due to improper notice) is a CTL blocker.

Federal Tax Liens (IRS): The IRS has a 120-day right of redemption after foreclosure of a property with a recorded federal tax lien (26 USC Section 7425). During this 120-day period, the property may not be listed. After the redemption period expires without IRS action, the lien is extinguished. If within the 120-day window, CTL verdict must be NeedsHumanReview.

State and Local Tax Liens: Property tax liens take priority in all states. Delinquent property taxes must be paid before listing. State income tax liens or franchise tax liens vary by state but generally are CTL blockers if they remain after foreclosure.

Mechanic's Liens: Liens filed by contractors for unpaid work on the property. Mechanic's liens exceeding $2,500 are CTL blockers requiring resolution. Liens below $2,500 allow ClearWithConditions. Verify the lien amount and whether the lien filing deadline has passed per state statute (varies from 60 to 180 days from last work performed).

Judgment Liens: Civil court judgments recorded against the former owner may have attached to the property. In most states, judgment liens against the former owner are extinguished by foreclosure of a senior lien. Verify with title company. Any judgment lien that survived is a CTL blocker.

Lis Pendens: An active lis pendens (notice of pending litigation) filed against the property is a CTL blocker. The property may not be listed while active litigation is pending. If the lis pendens has been released, withdrawn, or the underlying action dismissed, obtain documentation and proceed.

Section 3 — Title Insurance:
A commitment for title insurance should be obtainable before listing. If a title company is unwilling to issue a commitment due to unresolved title issues, the property is not ready for CTL clearance. Common exceptions that do not block title insurance commitment include: standard utility easements, recorded subdivision restrictions, and zoning ordinances.

Section 4 — Chain of Title Issues:
Breaks in the chain of title (e.g., missing assignments, unrecorded deeds, estate transfers without probate) must be resolved through curative documents before listing. Common curative actions include: recording missing assignments of mortgage, obtaining corrective deeds, completing affidavits of heirship, and quiet title actions. A quiet title action typically takes 60 to 120 days and constitutes a CTL blocker until resolved.

Section 5 — Environmental Liens:
Environmental liens filed by EPA, state environmental agencies, or municipalities for contamination cleanup costs are CTL blockers. These liens survive foreclosure in most jurisdictions under CERCLA (42 USC Section 9607). Properties with environmental liens require NeedsHumanReview with environmental counsel consultation before any listing decision.

References: General title examination standards. 26 USC Section 7425 (IRS redemption). 42 USC Section 9607 (CERCLA environmental liability). State-specific lien priority and foreclosure statutes.
